Marks: **(M1)** method, **(A1)** accuracy, **(B1)** independent. Total **32**.

::: {.callout-important}
## What to watch while marking

1. **Is every "false" backed by a number?** "It does not always work" is not a counterexample.
2. **Did a "for every $n$" argument cover every residue?** Checking $n=1,2,3$ and stopping is the usual gap.
3. **Question 7(b) is the discriminating one.** The conclusion is true and the argument is still unsound —
   students who say "true, so the argument is fine" have missed the whole point of fact 16.
:::

# Section A — Recall

## Question 1 **[4]**

::: {.question}
Complete: (a) primes $>3$ have the form \_\_\_ and the converse fails at \_\_\_; (b) Euclid's lemma needs
$p$ to be \_\_\_, else \_\_\_; (c) remainder condition; (d) a composite $N$ has a prime factor at most \_\_\_.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer

**(a) $6n\pm1$; smallest counterexample $25$. (B1)** *($25=6(4)+1$ is of the right form and is not prime.
Accept $35$ or $49$.)* The implication runs prime $\Rightarrow6n\pm1$, **never** backwards.

**(b) Prime; $4\mid2\times2$ but $4\nmid2$. (B1)** *Accept any composite $a$ with $a\mid bc$, $a\nmid b$,
$a\nmid c$ — but $a=4,b=c=2$ is the smallest.*

**(c) $0\le r<a$. (B1)** The size condition is half the definition; without it $r$ is merely "something
left over".

**(d) $\sqrt N$. (B1)** *If $N=ab$ with $1<a\le b$ then $a\le\sqrt N$, and some prime divides $a$.*

**Marking.** (a) and (b) need **both** halves for the mark.
:::

---

## Question 2 **[4]**

::: {.question}
True or false, with a counterexample for each false one: (a) $12\mid n^2\Rightarrow12\mid n$;
(b) $n^2\equiv2\pmod3$ possible; (c) irreducible $\Rightarrow$ prime values; (d) $\gcd(n,n+1)=1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer

**(a) False. (B1)** $n=6$: $n^{2}=36=12\times3$, yet $12\nmid6$. *Squaring doubles exponents, so $n^{2}$
carrying $2^{2}\cdot3$ only forces $n$ to carry $2\cdot3$.*

**(b) False. (B1)** Squares are $0$ or $1$ mod $3$ — never $2$. *(Residues: $0^2=0$, $1^2=1$,
$2^2=4\equiv1$.)*

**(c) False. (B1)** $x^{2}+1$ is irreducible over $\mathbb Z$, but at $x=3$ it is $10=2\times5$. *Accept
$3x^{2}+3x+1$ at $x=5$, giving $91=7\times13$.*

**(d) True. (B1)** Any common divisor of $n$ and $n+1$ divides their difference, which is $1$.

**Marking.** A verdict with no counterexample scores **0** for that part.
:::

# Section B — Standard

## Question 3 **[4]**

::: {.question}
(a) Show $12\mid n^{2}\iff6\mid n$. (b) Hence a value with $12\mid n^{2}$ but $12\nmid n$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer

### (a) **[3]**

**($\Leftarrow$) (M1)** If $6\mid n$, write $n=6m$. Then $n^{2}=36m^{2}=12\left(3m^{2}\right)$, so
$12\mid n^{2}$. ✓

**($\Rightarrow$) (M1 A1)** Suppose $12\mid n^{2}$, i.e. $2^{2}\cdot3\mid n^{2}$.

- $3$ is **prime** and $3\mid n^{2}$, so $3\mid n$ *(Euclid's lemma — fact 2)*.
- $4\mid n^{2}$ forces $n$ to be even: if $n$ were odd, $n^{2}$ would be odd. So $2\mid n$.

Having both $2\mid n$ and $3\mid n$ with $\gcd(2,3)=1$ gives $6\mid n$. ∎

*Accept the exponent argument instead:* $n^{2}$ carries only even powers, so $2^{2}\mid n^{2}$ needs just
$2^{1}\mid n$, and $3^{1}\mid n^{2}$ needs $3^{1}\mid n$ (since the power in $n^2$ is even and at least 1,
hence at least 2).

### (b) **[1]**

**$n=6$. (B1)** $n^{2}=36$ is divisible by $12$, but $6$ is not. *(Accept $18$, $30$, any $6k$ with
$12\nmid6k$.)*
:::

## Question 4 **[4]**

::: {.question}
(a) Show $n^{2}\equiv0$ or $1\pmod4$. (b) Hence no $4k+3$ is a square, and $a^{2}+b^{2}=4k+3$ has no
integer solutions.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer

### (a) **[2]**

**Split by parity. (M1)**

- $n=2m$: $n^{2}=4m^{2}\equiv0\pmod4$.
- $n=2m+1$: $n^{2}=4m^{2}+4m+1=4m(m+1)+1\equiv1\pmod4$.

So $n^{2}\equiv0$ or $1$ — never $2$ or $3$. **(A1)** ∎

### (b) **[2]**

**No square is $4k+3$ (B1)** — immediate from (a), since $4k+3\equiv3$.

**The sum of two squares. (B1)** Each of $a^{2}$ and $b^{2}$ is $0$ or $1$ mod $4$, so
$$a^{2}+b^{2}\equiv0+0,\;0+1,\;1+0\text{ or }1+1\equiv0,\,1\text{ or }2\pmod 4 .$$
It can **never** be $3$. Hence $a^{2}+b^{2}=4k+3$ has no integer solutions. ∎

*This is the cleanest illustration of fact 5: a whole family of equations is killed without factorising
anything.*
:::

---

## Question 5 **[4]**

::: {.question}
(a) $720$ as prime powers and its divisor count. (b) Prove $d(N)$ odd $\iff N$ a perfect square.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer

### (a) **[2]**

**(M1)** $720=16\times45=2^{4}\cdot3^{2}\cdot5$.

**(A1)** $d(720)=(4+1)(2+1)(1+1)=5\cdot3\cdot2=\boxed{30}$.

### (b) **[2]**

**(M1)** With $N=p_1^{a_1}\cdots p_k^{a_k}$, $d(N)=(a_1+1)\cdots(a_k+1)$. A product of integers is **odd**
exactly when **every** factor is odd, i.e. every $a_i+1$ is odd, i.e. every $a_i$ is **even**.

**(A1)** Every exponent even $\iff N=\left(p_1^{a_1/2}\cdots p_k^{a_k/2}\right)^{2}$, i.e. $N$ is a perfect
square. ∎

*The pairing argument earns full marks too:* divisors come in pairs $d\leftrightarrow N/d$, and the count
is odd exactly when one divisor is its own partner, i.e. $d=\sqrt N$.
:::

## Question 6 **[4]**

::: {.question}
(a) Why $2^{n}-1$ prime forces $n$ prime. (b) A prime $n<15$ with $2^{n}-1$ composite. (c) What $341$ says
about Fermat as a primality test.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer

### (a) **[2]**

**(M1)** Suppose $n$ is composite, $n=ab$ with $a,b>1$. Then

$$2^{ab}-1=\left(2^{a}-1\right)\left(2^{a(b-1)}+2^{a(b-2)}+\cdots+2^{a}+1\right).$$

**(A1)** Since $a>1$, the first factor $2^{a}-1\ge3$; since $b>1$, the second factor is at least
$2^{a}+1\ge5$. Both exceed $1$, so $2^{n}-1$ is **composite**. Contrapositive: $2^{n}-1$ prime
$\Rightarrow n$ prime. ∎

### (b) **[1]**

**$n=11$. (B1)** $2^{11}-1=2047=23\times89$.

### (c) **[1]**

**(B1)** Passing the test proves **nothing**: $341=11\times31$ is composite yet satisfies
$2^{340}\equiv1\pmod{341}$. Fermat's little theorem gives a **necessary** condition for primality, never a
sufficient one — so it can only ever *disprove* primality.

*This is the T1 theme in one line:* the useful tests in this topic are all necessary-not-sufficient.
:::

# Section C — Stretch

## Question 7 **[4]**

::: {.question}
(a) Prove $6\mid n^{3}-n$. (b) "It factorises, so it is never prime" — is the conclusion true? Is the
argument sound?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer

### (a) **[3]**

**Factorise. (M1)** $n^{3}-n=n\left(n^{2}-1\right)=(n-1)\,n\,(n+1)$ — three **consecutive** integers.

**Divisible by $2$. (A1)** Among any two consecutive integers one is even, so $2$ divides the product.

**Divisible by $3$. (A1)** Among any three consecutive integers one is a multiple of $3$.

Since $\gcd(2,3)=1$, the product is divisible by $6$. ∎

*Accept the residue version:* check $n\equiv0,1,2\pmod3$ and $n\equiv0,1\pmod2$ separately.

### (b) **[1]**

**(B1)** **The conclusion is true, but the argument is not sound** — and the mark is for saying both.

- *True:* $n^{3}-n$ is $0$ at $n=-1,0,1$ and a multiple of $6$ otherwise, so it is never prime.
- *Unsound:* "it factorises, therefore it is never prime" is exactly the fallacy of fact 16 — a
  factorisation of the **expression** only makes the **value** composite if **both factors exceed $1$**.
  Here $n=2$ gives $1\cdot2\cdot3$, and the first factor **is** $1$; the argument as written would equally
  "prove" that $x^{2}-1=(x-1)(x+1)$ is never prime, which is false at $x=2$ where it equals $3$.

**Marking.** "True, so the argument works" scores **0**. The point is that a correct conclusion does not
validate the reasoning.
:::

## Question 8 **[4]**

::: {.question}
$p$ prime, $p>3$. (a) Why is $p$ odd and not a multiple of $3$? (b) Prove $24\mid p^{2}-1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer

### (a) **[1]**

**(B1)** $p>3$ and prime, so its only divisors are $1$ and $p$. If $2\mid p$ then $p=2$, contradiction;
if $3\mid p$ then $p=3$, contradiction. So $p$ is odd and $3\nmid p$.

### (b) **[3]**

**Factorise. (M1)** $p^{2}-1=(p-1)(p+1)$, and $p-1,\;p,\;p+1$ are three consecutive integers.

**The factor $8$. (A1)** $p$ is odd, so $p-1$ and $p+1$ are **consecutive even numbers**. One of any two
consecutive evens is divisible by $4$, so their product carries $2\times4=8$.

**The factor $3$. (A1)** One of the three consecutive integers is divisible by $3$; by (a) it is not $p$,
so it is $p-1$ or $p+1$ — either way $3\mid(p-1)(p+1)$.

Since $\gcd(8,3)=1$, we get $24\mid p^{2}-1$. ∎

*Check:* $p=5\Rightarrow24$; $p=7\Rightarrow48$; $p=11\Rightarrow120$; $p=13\Rightarrow168$ — all
multiples of $24$. ✓

**Marking.** The $8$ is the hard half. "$p-1$ and $p+1$ are both even so we get $4$" earns the method mark
but not the accuracy mark — *consecutive* evens give $8$, not $4$.
:::

---

::: {.callout-tip}
## The thread running through this paper

Questions 6(c), 7(b) and 8 are the same idea from three angles: **a condition that is necessary is not
therefore sufficient**, and **a true conclusion does not validate the argument that reached it**. Those two
sentences are what T1 is for; the arithmetic is incidental.
:::

:::
